playbook:
When a season begins, I check the stated sustainable share and take at or just under it unless I have a specific reason to deviate — keeping the stock high is what keeps future seasons profitable, and my final-season total is capped by early depletion.

In early seasons I do not over-harvest to "gain an edge." Grabbing a few extra fish early costs compounded regrowth across all remaining seasons and invites rivals to do the same; my fully cooperative run kept the stock pinned at 100 and paid off.

When I see rivals consistently landing above the sustainable share, I raise my own catch slightly above my share to avoid subsidizing their greed — I don't get out-competed while alone preserving the commons.

I watch each season's landed figures, not just the stock. If everyone's share is near the sustainable number, I stay cooperative; if someone defects upward, I nudge up a point or two rather than matching their full defection, which would race the stock to zero.

A small late defection by a rival (like 12.5 instead of 11.1 in season 5) is a signal they're positioning for the endgame grab — I note it but don't overreact mid-game; the correct response is a firm final-season catch, not a mid-game escalation that depletes the stock.

In the final season, the stock no longer needs to regrow, so I compute the stock divided by the number of boats and take roughly that (or a touch more) — that's my fair share of a stock that's about to be worthless. In my episode stock/3 was ~32.6 and I took 30; next time I take the full computed share or slightly above if rivals have behaved meekly.

Even in the final season I never exceed what remains available divided realistically among boats — a zeroed stock forfeits everything, so I leave a small buffer rather than taking the entire stock myself.

I keep a running idea of the terminal value: the last season's remaining stock divided among boats is roughly free fish, so I aim to arrive at the endgame with the stock healthy rather than grabbing early — the payoff of restraint shows up at the finish, not the start.

Playbook for catch (ref_commons):

- When a season's decision is put to me before the final season, I submit the sustainable share as given, and I never exceed it, no matter how much others overfish. Small defections by rivals (a few points above the share) don't destroy the stock; my defection adds nothing but risk. Confirmed: five seasons at 11.1 built a base of 55.5 while the stock stayed at 100.
- I don't try to punish or match overfishers. Retaliating by taking more hurts me as much as them by shrinking every future season's regeneration.
- I watch the stock trajectory, not just my rivals' catches. If the stock is declining season over season, I consider dropping slightly below the sustainable share only when the decline threatens collapse before the end — otherwise holding the share is enough.
- When the final season is put to me, I stop conserving and extract hard, since nothing left in the water scores. Two points now confirmed: first, a timid grab leaves free fish on the table; second, taking roughly a full one-third of the remaining stock works — I took 32 of 97.9 and landed essentially all of it (final score close to my submitted total). Next time I go even a touch bolder: rivals who conserved all game tend to stay moderate in the endgame, so one-third plus a margin (aiming for the stock divided by the number of boats, rounded up) is the right target — but never more than the stock itself, and I should expect that if every boat grabs, landings may be scaled down in order or pro rata, so submitting high costs nothing and protects me against rivals doing the same.
- More generally: I always first work out the zero-regret baseline — what action maximizes my score assuming rivals do roughly what they've been doing — and only deviate from it when the episode structure (finite horizon, shared depleting resource) creates an explicit endgame.
- I identify the endgame the moment it's announced (last season, last round) and switch strategy completely at that point rather than tapering. Switching only in season 6, not before, was correct: rivals stayed at the sustainable share right through season 5, so early defection would only have cost me.
- I keep replies short and always end with the exact bracketed token required.

2.text:
- When the fishery opens and I have no information about the other boats, I submit exactly the sustainable share. It protects the stock, establishes me as cooperative, and costs little at a full stock.
- When the history shows all boats fishing sustainably, I keep fishing sustainably rather than being the first to defect — cooperation from everyone is worth more than a small grab.
- When one boat is overfishing and the stock shows it, I fish modestly above the sustainable share rather than either absorbing their defections passively or matching their escalation. A 10–15% overshoot closes the gap without visibly triggering a race.
- When I deviate above the sustainable share, I remember that the harbour records my figure: my season-5 bump to 12.5 was visible in the history, and even though nobody retaliated, every boat saw it. I assume any overshoot can be read and factor that into how much edge-taking I expect to get away with before others respond.
- When the stock stays comfortably high with only a couple of seasons left, I loosen restraint slightly, because the remaining runway is the last value I can convert into catch — but I now start counting down from the middle seasons rather than waiting, since the cooperative periods in this episode left a large, unclaimed surplus that only the final season could partially capture.
- When the final season is put to me, I treat sustainability as worthless and submit the largest catch consistent with the other boats' plausible final-season aggression. My 40 against 97.9 stock was still too timid: two opponents who had never exceeded 12.5 were unlikely to take 30+ each, and I left dozens of fish unharvested. Next time I bound the others' grabs from their demonstrated behavior, take the stock minus that bound minus a thin safety margin, and scale the aggression up, not down, when the opponents have a long cooperative track record.
- When I calculate any season's catch, I first compute the total fishing pressure the recent history implies: if the other boats' current pace plus my planned catch would push the stock toward zero, I scale back regardless of my standing, because a collapsed fishery is a total loss — but I only shrink my margin for genuinely plausible rival grabs, not for ones their history never supports.
- I do not chase rank by matching the largest other's catch; I chase total landed fish. The record confirms steady sustainable play plus a final-season surge is the right structure — my loss was execution: the surge needs to be much larger, and the pre-endgame edge-taking can begin a season or two earlier when rivals show restraint.
